m: The highest point of achievement or excellence.
e: Greek akmē (point, peak, prime).
t: Akmē = the peak. (Yes, the Acme company in the Road Runner cartoons claims to be the best.)

e: Latin affabilis (easy to speak to): ad + fari (to speak).
t: Same as « affable »: easy to speak to.

e: Latin affluentem, from affluere (to flow towards): ad + fluere.
t: Money flowing towards you. In French « un affluent » is a tributary river; same flow image.

e: Old French amiable, from Late Latin amicabilis (friendly), from amicus.
t: Ami → amiable. « À l’amiable » = settled in a friendly way.

e: Old Norse bleikr (pale, shining), related to Old English blāc (pale). Germanic.
t: Pale and colourless, like a bleak winter landscape or a bleak outlook.

e: Latin candidus (white, pure). Roman office-seekers wore white togas, hence candidate.
t: Pure white: nothing hidden. French « candide » means naive; English candid means frank.

m: To suppress unacceptable parts of a text or film.
e: Latin censor, the Roman magistrate who took the census and policed morals, from censere (to assess).
t: Censor = cuts content. Censure (Common I) = formal blame.

e: de- + mean (low, inferior; Old English gemǣne, common). Germanic + Latin prefix.
t: Make someone mean (low). A demeaning task.

e: Probably Anglo-French demuré, from demorer (to stay, be calm), Latin demorari.
t: Demure = « sage comme une image ». Not demur (to object).

m: Characteristic of the devil; very bad.
e: Greek diabolos (slanderer, devil), from diaballein (to throw across, slander).
t: Same as « diabolique »: the devil (diable).

m: To follow closely and persistently; to plague.
e: Old English docga, a word of unknown origin. The verb (to track like a hound) dates from the 1500s.
t: A dog on your heels: dogged by scandal = « poursuivi par ».

m: To deceive; a person easily tricked.
e: French dupe, perhaps from huppe (hoopoe), a bird reputed to be stupid.
t: Same as French « duper ».

m: Deeply involved in a conflict or difficult situation.
e: French embrouiller (to confuse, tangle): en + brouiller.
t: « Embrouillé »: tangled up in a scandal.

e: Latin errare (to wander, stray).
t: To err is human: « l’erreur est humaine ».

e: Latin erraticus (wandering), from errare.
t: Wandering all over: « erratique ».

e: Old English hund (dog), Germanic (German Hund).
t: Hunted by hounds: the press hounded the minister.

m: To formally accuse of a crime.
e: Anglo-French enditer, from Latin indicere (to proclaim): in + dicere (to say). Pronounced “in-DITE”.
t: Indicere = to declare against. Silent c: in-DITE.

e: Late Latin indigenus, from indigena (native): indu (within) + gignere (to beget).
t: Born within: « autochtone ».

e: Latin indignari (to consider unworthy): in- + dignus (worthy).
t: Same as « indigné »: « Indignez-vous ! »

e: Latin inflammare (to set on fire), from flamma.
t: Words that set the room on fire: « des propos incendiaires ».

e: in- + Latin solvere (to loosen, pay).
t: Not solvable: « insolvable ».

e: Latin inundare: in + unda (wave).
t: Unda = onde: « inonder ». Inundated with emails.

e: French macabre, from Danse Macabre (Dance of Death, 15th c.), perhaps after the Maccabees.
t: La Danse macabre: skeletons dancing. Same as French.

e: From Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815), a German doctor whose “animal magnetism” sessions were the rage in Paris.
t: Picture Mesmer’s Parisian salons, patients entranced around his tub.

m: A person who hoards wealth and spends little.
e: Latin miser (wretched, unhappy).
t: Latin miser = « misérable »: the wretched hoarder (Harpagon, Scrooge).

e: Probably per- (thoroughly) + use: to use up completely.
t: Per + use = use thoroughly. On the GRE: careful reading.

m: To long for; to waste away from grief.
e: Old English pīnian (to torment), from Latin poena (punishment).
t: Poena = peine: pining for a lost love.

e: Old French pinacle, from Late Latin pinnaculum (peak, turret), from pinna (feather, point).
t: « Porter au pinacle »: the turret at the very top.

e: Latin profusus, from profundere (to pour out).
t: Pouring forth: profuse apologies.

e: Latin remissus (slack), from remittere (to send back, relax).
t: Slackened off: it would be remiss of me not to thank…

e: Late Latin reprobatus (rejected), from reprobare (to disapprove).
t: « Les réprouvés »: those rejected by God.

e: From retire, French retirer (to withdraw).
t: Someone who withdraws (« se retire ») from the crowd.

m: A long, tedious, usually angry piece of writing.
e: Old English scrēade (a shred, strip). A long strip of parchment.
t: A long shred of paper full of ranting.

e: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 from the Persian tale The Three Princes of Serendip (Sri Lanka), who kept making lucky discoveries.
t: The princes of Serendip finding treasures by accident. Fleming’s penicillin.

e: English slap + dash, both suggesting quick, careless action.
t: Slap it on, dash off: « travail bâclé ».

m: A person who spends money wastefully.
e: spend + thrift (savings, prosperity, from Old Norse þrift). Someone who spends the savings.
t: Spends the thrift (the savings).

m: A fixed regular allowance or salary.
e: Latin stipendium (soldier’s pay): stips (coin) + pendere (to weigh out).
t: Coins weighed out for a soldier. PhD stipend.

m: The highest point; a meeting of leaders.
e: Old French somete, diminutive of som, from Latin summum (highest).
t: « Sommet » and « sommet du G7 ».

e: From tell, Old English tellan (to count, relate). Germanic.
t: It tells you something. A telling silence.

e: tell + tale: originally a tattletale who tells tales.
t: Telltale signs = « signes révélateurs ».

m: To offer formally (tender a resignation); money offered.
e: Old French tendre (to offer, stretch out), from Latin tendere.
t: « Tendre la main »: you stretch out an offer. Legal tender, a public tender (appel d’offres).

e: thorough (Old English þuruh, through) + going. Going all the way through.
t: Going thoroughly through everything.

e: From thrift, Old Norse þrift (prosperity), from thrive.
t: Thrifty people thrive. A thrift shop sells cheap second-hand goods.

m: A long angry speech of criticism.
e: French tirade, from Italian tirata (a pull, volley), from tirare (to pull).
t: Same as « tirade » (Cyrano’s famous nose tirade).

e: under + write: insurers wrote their names under the risk on Lloyd’s policies.
t: Signing your name under a policy to cover it. Banks underwrite an IPO.

m: To make someone lose courage or confidence.
e: un- + nerve (strength, courage), from Latin nervus (sinew).
t: Remove the nerve (courage): his stare unnerved me.

e: Latin variantia, from variare (to change).
t: At variance with = « en désaccord avec ». Also statistical variance.

m: Having a strong desire for revenge.
e: From Latin vindicta (vengeance), from vindicare.
t: Same as « vindicatif ».

e: Latin vorax, from vorare (to devour).
t: « Dévorer »: a voracious reader.

e: Arabic samt ar-ra’s (path over the head), misread by medieval scribes as cenit.
t: Same as « zénith »: the sun right over your head.
